title: How to iron a cross-stitch piece
subtitle: Pressing the fabric flat without crushing the stitches or distorting the weave
excerpt: Ironing a cross-stitch piece removes creases from the fabric and sets the stitches neatly without flattening them. The key is to work face-down on a thick soft surface so the stitches sink into the padding rather than being pressed flat by the iron, and to move the iron parallel to the fabric threads rather than across them.
sourceNotes: Textile finishing practice for embroidered needlework. Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive. Standard finishing guidance in cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: Ironing a finished cross-stitch piece sets the

flat and removes any crease from hooping or storage. The stitches must not be touched by the iron directly; they would flatten and lose their texture. Work face-down on a thick padded surface so the stitches sink into the padding and the heat reaches the fabric from behind.

Lay a clean white towel on the ironing board. Place the finished piece face-down on the towel, stitches against the towel surface. The towel acts as padding so the stitches press into it rather than being crushed flat.
If the piece is dry, lightly mist the back of the fabric with water or use a steam iron set to the cotton or linen setting. Slightly damp fabric takes a crease out more easily than bone-dry fabric.

Press the iron on the back of the fabric, moving in straight lines parallel to the threads of the weave. Work outward from the centre. Do not press across the grain; it pulls the weave and distorts the squares.
Lift the iron rather than sliding it across the stitched area. A sliding motion drags threads. Lift, move, press.

Turn the piece over and check from the front. The stitches should look raised and defined, and the fabric should be smooth and flat with no creases remaining. If creases remain, repeat on the back with a little more steam.

items.symptom: Stitches look flat and shiny after ironing
items.cause: The iron was placed directly on the stitched side, or the pressing cloth was too thin.
items.fix: Always press face-down on a thick padded surface. If the stitches have been flattened, try steaming the piece face-up, holding the iron a few centimetres above the surface, to lift the threads without pressing them.

items.symptom: The fabric warped or stretched after ironing
items.cause: The iron was moved across the grain of the weave, or too much pressure was applied to a single area.
items.fix: Dampen the piece again and re-block it: pin it to a foam board in the correct dimensions and let it dry. Then press again from the back, working parallel to the weave.

content.text: A pressed piece is ready to mount or frame. For lacing onto card, a flat and square piece is much easier to work with than a creased one. Mount while the fabric is still slightly damp from the steam if you need to stretch it onto a mount board.
